summary:
The Republic of the Congo does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct between adults. A systematic legislative review published by the European Union Agency for Asylum in May 2024 reached that finding, and the United States Department of State human rights reports for 2022 and 2023 record the same position. Same-sex relationships have been legal since 1940.

Penal Code Article 331, as amended in 2006, sets an unequal age of consent: 21 years for same-sex acts against 18 years for different-sex acts. It punishes 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under 21 with six months to three years imprisonment and a fine. The EUAA review, drawing on ILGA data, and the State Department reports describe the scope of that provision as applied to same-sex conduct as ambiguous, and sources treat it as a basis for justifying discrimination.

Prosecutions under Article 331 are not documented. The State Department recorded no known arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the provision during 2023. Police nonetheless invoke it as a pretext to solicit bribes from men perceived as gay, and officers have falsely claimed that same-sex activity is generally illegal in order to extract money. Such abuses are rarely reported because of fear of police interaction, and are investigated when they are reported.

There is no legally recognised procedure for changing gender identity in the Republic of the Congo. A trans visitor whose passport, visa or other identity documents carry a gender marker that does not match their presentation has no local route to obtain congruent documentation, and no legal protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity.

Marriage is defined in Section 2, Article 127 of the Family Code as a public act establishing a lasting union between a man and a woman, which explicitly bars recognition of same-sex marriage. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed as same-sex under birth-sex status has no prospect of local recognition.

No broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation exists, and there are no hate crime laws, so a visitor has no statutory discrimination or bias-crime route to pursue.

Violence and harassment against LGBTQI+ people are documented. Non-governmental organisations reported psychological and physical harassment and financial extortion by both government actors and nonstate actors. Violence rose in 2022, a trend attributed to forced confinement during the COVID-19 pandemic and to worsening economic hardship, and most of it was committed by family members. State authorities and private citizens committed violence in 2022 and 2023. Where violence is reported, law enforcement punishes it.

Social attitudes are hostile. In a survey conducted between 2021 and 2023, 73 percent of residents of Brazzaville said they would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour.

Legal protections for sensitive personal data cover sexual orientation and sexual life but not gender identity. Article 19 of Law No. 27-2020 on the fight against cybercrime prohibits placing or storing personal data revealing sexual orientation without a legal exception or express consent, punishable by one to five years in prison, a fine of one million to ten million CFA francs, or both. Articles 8, 10 and 15 of Decree No. 2025-66 on the personal data of air passengers protect sexual orientation, and Articles 4, 14 and 40 of Law No. 29-2019 on the protection of personal data protect sexual life as sensitive personal data.
tangentialFactors:
Article 331's scope as applied to same-sex conduct is described as ambiguous by the EUAA review and the State Department reports. The provision is not used for arrests, yet sources treat it as a basis for justifying discrimination, which leaves the formal legal exposure of a relationship falling within its terms unresolved.

Violence against LGBTQ+ people rose in 2022, a shift attributed to forced confinement during the COVID-19 pandemic and to increasing economic hardship. Most of that violence was committed by family members.

A 2010 baseline linked social stigma to the absence of any significant gay or lesbian community presence, with no cases of violence or discrimination reported to non-governmental organisations or news media at that time, though instances may have gone unreported.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ civil society organisations were present in 2023 but had been unable to obtain legal recognition. In 2020 a non-governmental organisation was denied registration until references to its focus on the LGBTQ+ community were removed.

Residents have no legal route to change gender identity. No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and none covers education, healthcare, housing or employment. There are no hate crime laws, and no law regulates conversion therapy or surgery on intersex children intended to make their bodies conform to expected norms.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document societal tolerance of transgender people specifically. Tolerance and violence findings are framed around LGBTQ people generally or around homosexual neighbours, so the trans-specific risk picture is inferred from the wider legal and social regime rather than measured directly.

Article 331's scope as applied to same-sex conduct remains ambiguous. No court ruling, prosecution record or interpretive guidance resolving it was identified.

Violence findings in the sources are qualitative. No incident counts, rates or population denominators are given, so no comparison with the country's general violence level can be made.
